finding: "tp config --extract ... is resolution-preserving by construction: it hoists only a value every task file already carries, so what resolves is unchanged and the change rule never fires" is false, and the counterexample was BUILT AND RUN, not reasoned. --extract preserves resolution only for the task files it scanned; it silently changes it for every resolution context that has no task-level override. Measured in /tmp/tp-r12/extract with the dev binary on the shipped twin field review_converge_on (already in hoistedFields, so it is the exact mechanism row 4 adds audit_converge_on to): one task file spec/a.tasks.json carrying {"review_converge_on":"all"}, empty .tp/config.json, and a second spec spec/b.md with no task file. Before: `tp config --file spec/b.tasks.json --resolved` reports {source: default, value: blocking}. Then `TP_UNATTENDED=1 tp config --extract --force` exits 0 with {"hoisted":["review_converge_on"]}, writes the value into .tp/config.json and strips it from a.tasks.json. After: base b reports {source: project, value: all} — the resolved value CHANGED, unattended, exit 0, no refusal. Mapped onto this release: one task file legitimately carrying audit_converge_on: blocking (an attended, operator-approved opt-in the release is for) makes --extract write blocking into the project layer, and every base with no task-level override then resolves blocking. That is precisely the uncovering §3 says only tp import can do, performed by the one writer §3 exempts from the fence. It is reachable in this repository today: 21 of 46 spec/*.md have no .tasks.json (13 of them planned releases), and `tp audit spec/b.md --status` runs and resolves its workflow with no task file at all — verified, exit 0. It is also reachable with zero missing task files, because it is prospective: after the hoist, the NEXT tp init / tp import creates a task file whose workflow block is empty, and that base resolves blocking from the project layer without any fenced write ever happening. Note also that `tp config --extract --force` is not `tp import --force`: it is in no unattended decision set and was confirmed to exit 0 under TP_UNATTENDED=1.
suggestion: Delete the "by construction" exemption. Either (a) name --extract as a fourth FENCED write path — it is a two-layer write and the change rule is computable there, comparing resolved-before/resolved-after over every discovered base plus the bare project layer; or (b) exclude audit_converge_on from hoistedFields the way commit_strategy is already excluded (config_extract.go carries the precedent and the reason), and reverse §7 row 4 accordingly. Whichever is chosen, §7 needs a row whose mutant is the one just run: hoist from a tree where one base carries the value and another has no task file, and assert the second base's resolved value is unchanged. Row 4 as written asserts only that the field IS hoisted, which is the step that opens the hole.

finding: The fence is defined over "the resolved value", but resolution in tp is per task file — `engine.ResolveWorkflow(specPath, flagFile)` needs a spec path to reach the task-override layer, and this repository holds one `<base>.tasks.json` per version. "The resolved value" is therefore not single-valued for the two sinks that write below the task layer. §3's must-pass example — "a `--project` write of `blocking` beneath a task override of `all` changes nothing an audit will read and must pass" — is stated for a repo with exactly one task file. With two (T1 overriding `all`, T2 carrying no override) the same `tp set --project audit_converge_on=blocking` changes what T2 resolves and not what T1 resolves, and §3 gives no rule for which comparison the fence makes: any-spec, all-specs, or the active pointer's. `tp set --project` takes no spec argument, so the implementer must invent the enumeration. §7 row 13 pins only the single-task-file shape, so every choice passes the suite.
suggestion: State the quantifier in §3: the fence refuses when the write changes the resolved value to `blocking` for ANY task file discovered under the repository (plus the no-task-file resolution, which the project layer also governs), and say explicitly that `tp set --project` enumerates task files to evaluate it. Add a §7 row with two task files that differ in their override, asserting the refusal fires on the one that changes and pins which population is compared.

finding: This round's repair gives one refusal message two incompatible audiences. The same refusal fires for an authoring error (remedy: edit the document, and §3 requires the message to name the two forms that pass) and for a unit that intends the relax (remedy: `tp escalate --decision audit-converge-on`). A unit that meant to relax reads a message stating that carrying `"audit_converge_on": "all"` makes the import pass, does exactly that, and silently reverts an operator-approved `blocking` — no escalation, no round-trip, no record. §7 row 14 pins only that the message names the two documents and that it avoids the command-field wording, so a message that never mentions the escalation path passes every assertion in the release.
suggestion: Make the message name all three exits with the condition that selects each, or split the refusal by what changed: name the two documents when the resolved-before value was already `blocking` (the uncovering/authoring case), and name escalation when the write itself introduces the literal. Add a §7 row pinning that the message names the escalation path.

finding: §3 twice cites a table that this round deleted. Line 186 reads "a fence built from the three shapes in the table above would not", and §7 row 13b's mutant reads "build the fence from the three shapes in §3's table, which do not reach this input". §3 contains no table at all — the only tables in the file are at lines 43, 88, 121 and 333, none of them in §3, and the rejected-rules table was cut this round. Both references are load-bearing rather than decorative: row 13b's mutant is defined entirely as "the three shapes in §3's table", so with the table gone the row names no mutant an implementer can build, and §3's own argument for the change rule rests on a comparison against a set the reader cannot see.
suggestion: Either restore the three shapes inline in §3 (field-scoped / value-scoped / literal-transition, one clause each) and keep the two references, or rewrite both sentences to name the three narrower rules §3 already spells out in prose at lines 166-170 and drop the words "the table".

finding: §3's "resolution-preserving by construction" is false for a spec that has no task file, and that clause is the whole reason `tp config --extract` is exempted from the fence. Proven by running, not reading (tp built from HEAD at /tmp/tp-dev/tp): in a fresh git repo with a.md/b.md carrying `a.tasks.json`/`b.tasks.json` that both set a workflow field, plus lonely.md with NO task file, `TP_UNATTENDED=1 tp config --extract` exits 0 with no refusal and hoists the field into .tp/config.json; `tp config --resolved --file lonely.md` reports the field as `{source: default, value: 2}` before and `{source: project, value: 5}` after. Substituting `audit_converge_on`, the identical command changes lonely.md's resolved value from `all` to `blocking` — a relax of the gate, under the environment the fence exists for, with the change rule never firing because §3 asserts it cannot. The hole is not theoretical: 21 of this repository's 46 `spec/*.md` files have no `<base>.tasks.json` (counted). It also survives the import fence: once the project layer holds `blocking`, a later `tp import` for that spec compares resolved-before against resolved-after and sees no change, so row 13b's rule passes it.
suggestion: Either fence `tp config --extract` by the same resolved-change rule applied over every spec the repository holds (not only those with task files), or narrow the claim: "resolution-preserving for every spec that has a task file; a spec with none moves from the built-in to the hoisted value, so --extract is fenced for `audit_converge_on`". Add a §7 row with the mutant "exempt --extract because it hoists a unanimous value, which is resolution-preserving only over the specs it read".

finding: §3's claim that `tp config --extract` is "resolution-preserving by construction" holds only for the task files present at the moment of the hoist, and the fence has no clause for what happens afterwards. `hoistedFields`/`computeCommonPolicy` hoist a field only when every task file already carries the same value and then strip it from those files — so if every task file carries `blocking`, the extract writes `blocking` into `.tp/config.json`. Every task file created after that (by `tp init`, or by a decompose unit) carries no override and now resolves `blocking` from the project layer, in a cycle for which no human made the decision §3 says is human-only. The composite path is unfenced end to end: `tp config --extract` (no unattended fence, only a clean-tree gate) followed by any later `tp import`, whose change rule compares resolved-before `blocking` against resolved-after `blocking` and passes. §3's sentence "the sink that uncovers is `tp import`" is an exhaustive claim over the write paths and this falsifies it — `--extract` is a sink that uncovers on every future task file, not on the ones it hoisted from.
suggestion: Either fence `tp config --extract` under `TP_UNATTENDED=1` when the hoisted value is `blocking`, or exclude `audit_converge_on` from `hoistedFields` and say why (which contradicts §7 row 4, so pick one). If it is kept hoistable, replace "resolution-preserving by construction" with the accurate scope — preserving for the task files it hoisted from, and prospectively binding for every task file created afterwards — and add a §7 row for the extract-then-init sequence.

finding: §4 conditions `by_severity` on the rows rather than the policy, and justifies that entirely by `--merge`'s inability to resolve the workflow. But this release has two sinks that DO resolve it — §7 row 3 makes an invalid stored value fail at `tp audit --record` and `--status`, and §2 stamps `clean` at record time under the resolved policy — and neither is priced as the home for the breakdown. The consequence is paid by the default path: `all` is the default, §2.1 argues in 2 of 2 measured cycles that it should stay the default, and under `all` every non-`PASS` row already blocks, so the breakdown feeds no decision an agent makes. Every project therefore parses a new key on every merged round holding a non-`PASS` row, and row 16 makes it survive `--compact` — the surface whose whole job is to strip what the agent does not need.
suggestion: Price the alternative in §4: emit `by_severity` from `--record`/`--status`, which resolve the policy and already walk the round's rows, leaving `--merge` unchanged. If it must stay on `--merge`, justify the `all`-path cost by a decision an agent makes under `all`, not by the sink's limitation, and let `--compact` strip it there.

finding: The header epigraph names §6's own content as the example of what must not be in this file. It says a repository survey — "line-number citations, counted enumerations, which of eleven assertions survive" — belongs in task acceptance, not here. §6 item 1 is exactly that survey: "Two of the eleven `assert.`/`require.` call sites in `TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate` (`internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go`); the other nine stand — nine under that counting rule, which includes two `require.True(t, ok)` decode checks, and the rule is stated because without it the number is 7." §7 row 18 then pins the count of eleven as a test assertion, so the release both forbids the enumeration and normatively requires it. §6's own preamble makes the collision sharper: it says "the release owes the derivation instead of the count" and "the count has been one, two, three and five, and each number was falsified by the next round" — and then item 1 ships a new count of eleven with a bespoke counting rule to defend it. §6.5's measurements are different and the epigraph permits them ("measurements that justify a decision stay"); the eleven call sites justify no decision, they only describe a tree.
suggestion: Delete the call-site arithmetic from item 1 and state the decision instead — the guard must assert that `audit_converge_on` IS a known workflow field, and every other assertion in that test is unchanged. Move the count and its counting rule into the task's acceptance, where it is re-derived from the tree, and re-word §7 row 18 to assert the reversal and the absence of deletions without naming a total.

finding: §6's sweep predicate is scoped to "doc comments" and therefore does not reach the two shipped comments §2 names as false under `blocking`. §2 states: "Both audit sinks compute `next_action` from the round's `clean`, each carrying a comment asserting the equivalence this release breaks — that a round's non-`PASS` rows are exactly `!clean`." Verified in the tree: internal/cli/audit_record.go:124 ("The just-recorded round is the latest, so its non-PASS rows are exactly !clean.") and internal/cli/audit_record.go:389 ("The latest recorded round holding open non-PASS rows is exactly !Clean."). Both sit inside function bodies — neither is a doc comment, so neither is picked up by the acceptance sweep as written ("across `skills/`, `README.md`, `internal/engine/` and `internal/cli/` doc comments"), and no §7 row covers them. §6's whole design is that the count is untrustworthy and "the deliverable is the sweep, and the task's acceptance runs it rather than restating its result" — a sweep whose stated scope provably misses the two instances the release itself names in §2 cannot carry that weight, and both survive as shipped false assertions with the gate green.
suggestion: Widen the predicate's Go scope from "doc comments" to "comments" in `internal/engine/` and `internal/cli/`, and add a §7 row asserting that neither audit_record.go comment states the non-PASS/`!clean` equivalence, with the mutant "restrict the sweep to declaration doc comments, which leaves both call sites' comments false".

finding: §6.5 misstates the shipped caveat it exists to price, in both direction and extent. It says the object's "third message form counts rows carrying no `role` as `unattributed_open` and warns that the spec-coverage streak may be UNDERSTATED". The shipped strings in `engine.divergenceMessage` say the opposite: "none attributed to a role (possibly spec-coverage's)" and "(including %d with no role, which may be spec-coverage's)". The hazard they name is that an open row belongs to spec-coverage while `auditRoundOpenByRole` skips roleless rows, so spec-coverage is reported clean when it is not — the streak is OVERSTATED, not understated. The direction is the whole point: an understated streak delays a release, an overstated one ships over an unmeasured conformance failure, and §6.5 tells the operator they are accepting the harmless one. Extent is wrong too: two of the three message forms carry the caveat, not the third alone — the `unattributedOpen == otherRolesOpen` form carries it as well, and that is the form §6.5's own corpus produces (spec/.tp-review/0.23.0/audit-round-1.ndjson has one non-PASS row and it is roleless).
suggestion: Rewrite the sentence to say the caveat warns the spec-coverage streak may be OVERSTATED because a roleless open row may be spec-coverage's, and that two of the three message forms carry it. Then re-check the paragraph's conclusion: the price the release accepts is losing a warning about a possibly-false clean conformance streak, which is a larger claim than "understated" makes it look.

finding: Row 11's named mutant cannot fail row 11, and the fact it cites is false. The mutant is "count the streak as a total rather than a trailing run — v0.35.0 has three clean-under-`blocking` rounds before round 3, so a total reaches 2 one round early". Measured over spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/audit-round-*.ndjson, the clean-under-`blocking` rounds are 2,3,5,6,7,8,9 and the unclean ones are 1 (2 error) and 4 (1 error) — so exactly ONE clean round precedes round 3, not three. Because round 1 is unclean and rounds 2 and 3 are both clean, a total and a trailing run reach 2 at the same round. Replaying all eight cells row 11 asserts under both rules gives identical answers: blocking 3 / all 9 at audit_clean_rounds 2 and blocking 2 / all 8 at 1 for v0.35.0, and blocking 3 / all never at 2 and blocking 2 / all never at 1 for v0.36.0. A row whose mutant leaves every asserted number unchanged pins the trailing-run rule not at all, which §7's own preamble forbids.
suggestion: Replace the mutant with one the corpus can distinguish — the natural one is a streak that does not reset on an unclean round mid-history, which v0.35.0's round 4 (`error`) does discriminate for any assertion covering rounds 5-7 — or add a synthetic fixture with a clean/unclean/clean prefix and assert on it. Delete the "three clean rounds before round 3" claim; it is false on the data the row replays.

finding: Row 11's named mutant survives row 11, and I replayed it rather than reading it. The row asserts four convergence numbers and names as its mutant 'count the streak as a total rather than a trailing run', justified by 'v0.35.0 has three clean-under-blocking rounds before round 3'. Replaying the committed corpus (spec/.tp-review/0.35.0 and 0.36.0, 22 audit-round-*.ndjson files) under both counting rules gives identical results in all eight cells the row pins: v0.35.0 blocking 3/3, all 9/9; at audit_clean_rounds 1, 2/2 and 8/8; v0.36.0 blocking 3/3, all never/never. The reason is structural, not a fixture accident — a total and a trailing run first reach k at the same round, because they can only diverge after a clean round has already been followed by an unclean one, which is past the first convergence. The justification is also arithmetically impossible: only rounds 1 and 2 precede round 3, round 1 carries two error rows, so there is exactly ONE clean-under-blocking round before round 3, not three. §7's own preamble says every row 'names the mutant that must fail it'; the only row guarding §2.1 — the section that decides the release's default — names one that passes.
suggestion: Replace the mutant with one that actually reddens the numbers. Two that do: grade a non-PASS row with no usable severity as advisory (v0.35.0 round 4's rows carry error, so misgrading absent severity moves nothing, but the unrecognised fixtures of row 8 do) or, on the streak itself, 'treat a round with no non-PASS rows as clean under blocking WITHOUT checking severity' — which leaves all/blocking identical and reddens the blocking column in both cycles. Delete the 'three clean-under-blocking rounds' clause; the number is one.

finding: Row 11's rewritten mutant provably cannot fail row 11, and the sentence justifying it is arithmetically false. The cell reads "count the streak as a total rather than a trailing run — v0.35.0 has three clean-under-`blocking` rounds before round 3, so a total reaches 2 one round early". Measured over the committed corpus (per-round non-PASS severity counted from spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/audit-round-*.ndjson): v0.35.0's clean-under-`blocking` map is `. C C . C C C C C` — round 1 carries 2 `error` rows, so exactly ONE clean round precedes round 3, not three. And the mutant changes no answer anywhere in the row: computing both a trailing run and a running total over the same cleanmaps gives v0.35.0 blocking 3/3 at audit_clean_rounds 2 and 2/2 at 1, all 9/9 and 8/8; v0.36.0 blocking 3/3 and 2/2, all never/never. All eight of row 11's number pairs hold identically under the named mutant, so a correct replay and the mutant are indistinguishable at this row's observable. Round 11 reported this cell as a fixture variation rather than a mutant; the rewrite replaced it with a mutant that cannot fail, which is the same defect in the form §7's new column header forbids.

Two that do, checked against the same cleanmaps: "grade `error` as advisory" makes every v0.35.0 round clean under `blocking`, so the blocking column reads 2 instead of 3 and round 4's halt disappears; "treat a round with only `warning`/`info` rows as unclean under `blocking`" collapses the blocking column onto the `all` column (9 and never). Drop the three-clean-rounds sentence, which no cleanmap supports.

finding: Taking §2.1's own conclusion as given, the release never draws the ledger its lens requires. Against a measured yield of zero cycles in which the field would have been set correctly, it adds: a workflow field with two literals, validation at two sinks, an unattended fence across three write paths plus a fourth writer to reason about, a new `--decision` enum value, a new `--merge` key that survives `--compact`, a changed `AuditNextAction` signature with two new string forms, five reversed shipped assertions, and 26 test rows. §1 asserts of the fence that 'This is what the release buys' without ever naming what it is bought against.
suggestion: State the expected yield and the evidence for it — a cycle whose remaining rows were all advisory at the point the streak would have closed — or cut the surface to the field plus its two consuming sinks, deferring the fence, the enum value and the `--merge` key until a project actually sets the field.

finding: §1 says "Three deliverables" and then spends the ordinal "fourth" on the item that was CUT ("A fourth, a spec-hash reset ... is now `spec/0.46.0.md` §8.4"), while §6 opens with "This is work, not a Non-Goal" and receives five of §7's twenty-six test rows (18-22) — more rows than §4 and §3 combined. A decomposer sizing the release from §1, which is what §1 is for, sees three deliverables plus one deferral and misses a fifth of the test surface: a const rewrite, a doc-comment rewrite, two documentation rewrites, a guard-test reversal, a new guard assertion over REFERENCE.md, and a corpus-wide sweep across `skills/`, `README.md`, `internal/engine/` and `internal/cli/`. §6 explicitly says it is stated as its own section "because a decomposer reads the Non-Goals to learn what *not* to build" — the same reader reads §1 to learn what TO build, and §1 does not carry it.
suggestion: Make it four deliverables and give §6's sweep its own numbered entry in §1, naming the four surfaces it crosses. Refer to the cut spec-hash reset without an ordinal ("a fifth item, cut" or simply "a deferred item") so the word "fourth" is not held by something that does not ship.

finding: After this release the two twin fields carry the same two literals with opposite defaults, and no section says so. `engine.ResolveWorkflowLayers` defaults `review_converge_on` to `blocking` (configresolve.go: `ReviewConvergeOn: ReviewConvergeOnBlocking`), so review already ships with advisory findings not counted; §2 makes `audit_converge_on` default to `all`, the strict value. §1's opening sentence depends on the review default without naming it ("`review_converge_on` lets the review loop stop counting advisory findings" is true out of the box only because its default is `blocking`), and §2.1 argues the audit default at length without ever noting that the twin ships the opposite one. The consequence is on the reader of a config file: `review_converge_on` unset and `audit_converge_on` unset mean opposite policies, and §3's fence exists for one of them and not the other. §7 row 1 and row 2 assert structural parity (same precedence, same literals, same hint) which makes the divergence harder to notice, not easier.
suggestion: Add one sentence to §2.1 stating the asymmetry and why it is deliberate: review's relaxed value is its default because a review finding is advice, while an audit finding is a conformance claim, so audit opts in. Then check that §6's sweep clause (d) covers any shipped sentence that describes the two fields as behaving alike.

finding: The accepted count is delivered as a numeral inside the prose `next_action` string, while §4 states that the same population's count is already emitted machine-readably and unconditionally as `role_streaks[].open` on both `--status` and `--record`. The release therefore asks an agent to regex a number out of English that it can already sum from a key it parses anyway. The two differ only on roleless rows, which §6.5 says `auditRoundOpenByRole` drops — 20 of them across 90 recorded rounds — so the new channel exists to carry a delta of at most those rows. Row 10 then freezes the prose channel as a contract by pinning the numeral in the string.
suggestion: Emit the count as a key beside `next_action` and leave `next_action` a directive; or attribute roleless rows in `auditRoundOpenByRole` so the count is derivable from `role_streaks[].open` and add nothing. If the numeral stays in the string, state why an agent should parse prose for a number tp can key.

finding: The release refuses one disposition word and then adopts a stronger one in its own normative output. §2 says "*Surviving* is deliberately not the word: it would imply a disposition that removes a row from the count, which §5 declines to create" — and then §2's own next_action table says "when the round holds ACCEPTED rows" and "name the ACCEPTED count", §7 row 10 asserts "the count of accepted rows", and §7 row 19 puts the word into a SHIPPED constant: `engine.DivergenceHint` and SKILL.md are to say convergence counts every non-PASS row "the resolved policy does not ACCEPT". "Accepted" implies a per-row disposition at least as strongly as "surviving" does, and §5 item 2 says no such mechanism ships. The version in the shipped constant is the costly one: an agent reading "the resolved policy does not accept" will look for the accept/reject step and find none.
suggestion: Pick one vocabulary and use it in the table, in row 10, and in the replacement sentences. "Non-blocking" or "advisory" describes the population without implying an act: the table row becomes "name the count of non-blocking open rows" and row 19's sentence becomes "counts every non-PASS row of a blocking severity under the resolved policy" — but check that phrasing against row 19's own second mutant, which rules out "whose severity is blocking" for the `all` case, so the sentence needs the policy named rather than the severity.

finding: §2 decides two `next_action` branches this round and §7 tests one. The new table has two rows and the paragraph above it says "**Both affected branches are decided here rather than left to an implementer**, because this is the only place an operator learns that a round closed over open rows." Row 10 asserts only the converged arm: "a converged round holding non-`PASS` rows yields a `next_action` containing the count of accepted rows as a numeral". The other decided branch — clean, not yet converged — is `AuditNextAction`'s default arm (internal/engine/nextaction.go:82-83, "run the next audit round: tp audit …"), and it is the arm that fires on EVERY non-final round under `blocking`, where the converged arm fires once per cycle. No row covers it, and §7's closing "not tested here, named so the absence is deliberate" paragraph names only the three streak surfaces. An implementation that appends the count on the converged arm alone passes all 26 rows while leaving the common case as it is today.
suggestion: Extend row 10 to both arms — "on both audit sinks, both a converged round and a clean-but-not-yet-converged round holding non-`PASS` rows carry the count" — with the added mutant "append the count on the converged arm only, which leaves the arm an operator meets every round unchanged".

finding: §2 doubled its next_action decision this round and §7's row did not follow — the exact staleness §7's preamble exists to catch. Round 11 decided one branch ("The recommendation for that branch is decided here"); this round replaced it with a two-row table and the emphasis "**Both affected branches are decided here rather than left to an implementer**", covering (i) clean, not yet converged and (ii) clean, converged. Row 10 is byte-identical to round 11's and pins only branch (ii): "a CONVERGED round holding non-`PASS` rows yields a `next_action` containing the count of accepted rows as a numeral, textually different from an empty round's", with the mutant "branch on `clean` alone, which makes the two strings equal". Nothing pins branch (i), and it is the branch a `blocking` cycle hits repeatedly while the converged one fires once — v0.35.0 under `blocking` would take branch (i) on rounds 2 and every subsequent clean round, and branch (ii) once at round 3. Branch (i) is also the one where the implementation is easiest to get wrong: the default arm of engine.AuditNextAction is reached with `latestRoundHasFindings == false`, so an implementer who threads the count only through the converged case leaves it silently absent from the arm that runs most. The rest of §2's next_action decision checks out against the tree: AuditNextAction's signature is `(specPath string, converged, latestRoundHasFindings bool)`, it has exactly three branches in that precedence, both sinks derive the boolean from `clean` (audit_record.go:125 `!clean` and :390 `!rounds[len-1].Clean`, each carrying the comment §2 says asserts the equivalence), and the count §2 names is available on `--status` without re-reading role files because ReviewRound stores `Findings int`.
suggestion: Split row 10 into 10 and 10b, one per decided branch, each on both sinks — or widen row 10 to "on both audit sinks, BOTH clean branches (converged and not-yet-converged) holding non-PASS rows yield a next_action containing the count as a numeral" with the mutant "thread the count through the converged branch only, leaving the not-yet-converged arm textually identical to an empty round's". §2 names two branches; §7 should name two.

finding: §2 says `AuditNextAction` 'gains the count' and never says the boolean goes. `latestRoundHasFindings` is exactly `count > 0` under §2's own definition of the count (the latest recorded round's non-`PASS` rows), so the reading that keeps both makes every call site compute the same fact twice — and this repo enables `unparam`, so that reading does not merely waste bytes, it fails the quality gate. The stated justification, that 'the two facts the boolean folds together are now different questions', describes `clean` versus has-findings, which is not what the boolean carries; the boolean carries only has-findings.
suggestion: State the resulting signature literally — the boolean is replaced by the count — and make §7 row 10's subject the parameter list, so the mutant 'keep the boolean and pass `count > 0`' is visibly wrong rather than a defensible reading of the spec.

finding: §2 says the field is refused at the consuming sink 'on the same terms as review_converge_on', and row 3 pins that as an exit code. Measured, the two paths are not on the same terms and the difference is ordering, not wording. Built /tmp/tp-dev/tp from this tree and ran both sinks over identical trees whose task file stores an invalid converge value: `tp review spec.md --record f.ndjson` exits 1 and leaves NO .tp-review state at all — it resolves and validates before writing; `tp audit spec.md --record a.ndjson` exits 0, and .tp-review/spec/state.json holds round 1 with clean:false and the round file on disk. Reading internal/cli/audit_record.go shows why: `clean := findings == 0` is line 71, `recordAuditRoundEntry(..., findings, clean, ...)` is line 85, and `engine.ResolveWorkflow` is line 91 — the audit record path resolves the workflow AFTER the round is stored and validates this class of field nowhere. This release makes `clean` a function of the resolved policy, so the resolve must move above line 71; but row 3 asserts only an exit code, so an implementation that leaves the order alone and validates at line 91 passes row 3 while having already written a round whose clean byte was stamped under no policy. §2 makes that permanent — stamping is record-time and the only undo it names is 're-records the round', which appends.
suggestion: State in §2 that the audit record path resolves and validates audit_converge_on BEFORE it computes clean and before recordAuditRoundEntry, so a refused --record writes no round — the property tp review --record already has. finding: §2's `next_action` table and row 10 give different answers on the scenario §2 itself constructs two paragraphs earlier. finding: The one input the knob's decision needs — the previous cycle's severity mix — is served by a shell one-liner parked in `skills/tp/SKILL.md`, outside every tp surface the operator is already standing on, and §7 has no row for it, so it can rot without reddening anything. finding: This round deleted §3's three-row rule table (the round-11 snapshot carried it at what is now line 165) and replaced it with prose, but two references to that table survive and now resolve to the wrong thing or to nothing. A test whose subject the spec cannot name is a decision that has not been made yet"). finding: §3 adds `audit-converge-on` to the closed, validated `--decision` enum, but this round's repair removed its only described producer. finding: `by_severity` is emitted only when the round holds a non-`PASS` row, so its absence is ambiguous to the consuming agent: a clean round, or a tp older than v0.37.0. Disambiguating costs a version probe or a `by_status` cross-check on every merge — a round-trip paid on the common case to save a few bytes on the rounds that already carry the least output. suggestion: Emit `by_severity` unconditionally, as `{}` on an all-`PASS` round, and change row 15's assertion accordingly; or state in §4 how a consumer distinguishes 'clean round' from 'unsupported binary' and add a row pinning that.

finding: §4 states its problem on one command and ships its answer on another. The motivating sentence is "without it an agent reading `clean: true` cannot see what was suppressed" — but `clean` is emitted only by `tp audit --record` and (per round, inside `audit_rounds`) by `--status`; `tp audit --merge` never emits `clean` at all, and §4 is explicit that it cannot even resolve the policy. So the agent who reads `clean: true` on the gating sink still cannot see the breakdown, and the agent who can see the breakdown is looking at a payload with no verdict in it. §5 item 4 defers the record/status surface, which is a legitimate scope decision, but §4 then describes the merge-only breakdown as "the audit-side visibility this release ships" without saying that the visibility lands on a different command from the decision it is meant to inform — and `--merge` is optional in the audit loop as CLAUDE.md's Workflow D writes it.
suggestion: Rewrite §4's opening to name the actual reader: an agent running `--merge` immediately before `--record`, who sees the breakdown one command earlier than the verdict. Say plainly that a cycle which records without merging gets no breakdown, and that closing that gap is §5 item 4's deferral rather than something this release delivers.

finding: §4's premise for what is missing is false, and it makes three different populations share one name across the release. §4 says "The *count* of them is already emitted — `role_streaks[].open` is severity-blind and unconditional on both `--status` and `--record`". `role_streaks[].open` is a PER-ROLE count, not the round's total, and `engine.auditRoundOpenByRole` skips every row carrying no role — the exact 20 rows §6.5 counts and prices. So on a round holding roleless open rows the sum of `role_streaks[].open` is strictly less than the round's non-PASS count, and the count §4 says is "already emitted" is not. Meanwhile `--record` already emits the round total as `findings`, which §4 does not mention, and §2 defines the next_action count as a third phrasing, "the non-`PASS` rows of the latest recorded round". Three populations, one word, in one release — and §6.5 is the section that proves they differ.
suggestion: Correct §4's premise: on `--record` the round total is already emitted as `findings`; on `--status` it is recoverable from the stored round; `role_streaks[].open` is per-role and roleless-blind and is not that count. Then state once, in §2, which population `next_action`'s count and §4's buckets are over — the latest round's non-PASS rows including roleless ones — and say that this deliberately differs from the sum of `role_streaks[].open`.

finding: Row 19's prescribed replacement clause introduces exactly the word §2 refuses and the mechanism §5 declines. Rows 2 and 3 of §6 must be rewritten to say convergence counts every non-PASS row 'the resolved policy does not accept', and engine.DivergenceHint is a shipped constant that skills/tp/REFERENCE.md quotes verbatim, so that sentence ships to every operator. §2 explicitly rejects the synonym on this exact ground: 'Surviving is deliberately not the word: it would imply a disposition that removes a row from the count, which §5 declines to create.' 'Accept' implies the same disposition more strongly, because tp already ships a command that looks like it: `tp audit <file> --resolve <role>:<item> wontfix <reason>` runs today (internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go:480 exercises it), writes a `resolved` key on the row, and TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate exists precisely to prove that disposition does NOT stop the row counting. suggestion: Name the policy instead of a per-row verb: 'audit convergence counts every non-PASS row under audit_converge_on: all, and every row carrying a blocking severity under blocking.' finding: §6 makes the sweep the deliverable and the five-item list explicitly illustrative, but §7 pins only the five listed items (rows 18-21). finding: §6's headline change this round is that the count is replaced by a derivation the task's acceptance runs — but the derivation's scope clause does not reach two of the five items it is meant to subsume. Item 1's target is a TEST ASSERTION, not a doc comment: `assert.NotEqual(t, 0, code, "audit_converge_on is not a workflow field")` and `assert.Contains(t, stdout+stderr, "unknown workflow field: audit_converge_on")` in internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go — verified present, and the guard holds exactly eleven assert./require. call sites with exactly those two naming the field, as §6.1 says. Item 3's target is a `const`, not a doc comment: `engine.DivergenceHint` at internal/engine/divergence.go:16-19, whose final clause "audit convergence still counts every non-PASS row" was confirmed verbatim and is quoted verbatim by skills/tp/REFERENCE.md and asserted by internal/cli/docs_contract_test.go:145. Test files matter twice here: item 1 IS one, and items 2 and 3 are each held by a guard whose literal must move with the sentence, which the "three coordinated edits" paragraph already depends on.

finding: §6's preamble warns that "A sentence already covered by an item can carry a *second* false clause the item does not name" — and then items 2 and 4, the two largest, are each a one-clause repair of a sentence carrying four or five, with §7 rows 19 and 20 pinning only that one clause. Read against the tree. skills/tp/REFERENCE.md:754-756 is one sentence: "The audit gate is untouched: `engine.Converged`, `engine.ConsecutiveClean`, the stored per-round `clean` flag, the exit code of `tp audit --status --check`, and `next_action`'s three-state audit precedence all behave exactly as in v0.32.0." §2 lines 105-110 names ALL FIVE of those as changing under `blocking`. suggestion: Two edits. (1) Widen criterion (b) to the wording §2 already uses: "promises that `engine.Converged`, `engine.ConsecutiveClean`, the stored `clean` flag, `next_action` or the `--check` exit code is unchanged" — so the derivation covers every symbol the release's own downstream list names. finding: Row 22 pins the ABSENCE of a divergence object for roleless open rows, and its own mutant column says the change it forbids is `spec/0.46.0.md` §8's decision to make. finding: Row 11's mutant was rewritten this round and the replacement provably does not discriminate; the ground it cites is also false. The new column 4 reads "count the streak as a total rather than a trailing run — v0.35.0 has three clean-under-`blocking` rounds before round 3, so a total reaches 2 one round early". Both halves were measured against the recorded corpus, not reasoned. (a) v0.35.0 has ONE clean-under-`blocking` round before round 3, not three: round 1 carries {warning 5, info 5, error 2} and is unclean under blocking, round 2 carries {info 7, warning 5} and is clean. (b) Trailing-run and total-count convergence were computed side by side over the real per-round severity sequences of both cycles at both audit_clean_rounds values — all eight cells row 11 asserts are IDENTICAL under the two rules: v0.35.0 all 9/9, all@1 8/8, blocking 3/3, blocking@1 2/2; v0.36.0 all never/never, blocking 3/3, blocking@1 2/2. Applying the named mutant leaves every assertion in row 11 green, so the row cannot fail it. The reason is structural: the two rules can only differ after a break in the sequence, and in both cycles the first two clean rounds under each policy are adjacent. Round 11's version of this row named a different mutant ("replay with the field set at round k, which §2.1 says converges no earlier than k + audit_clean_rounds") which does discriminate, since §2.1's own second paragraph states the shift; the rewrite replaced a working mutant with one that cannot fail.
suggestion: Restore a mutant the fixture can kill. The set-at-round-k mutant is one (it moves v0.35.0/blocking from 3 to k+2). Another that discriminates on this corpus: grade blocking on `severity == "error"` alone instead of §2's fail-closed rule — v0.29.0-v0.32.0's 67 out-of-enum rows flip clean under it, though not v0.35.0/v0.36.0's, so the fixture would need to carry one. Whichever is chosen, delete the "three clean-under-blocking rounds" sentence: it is a counted claim the corpus falsifies, and §7's preamble asks each row to state the counting rule it depends on, not to assert an uncounted number.

finding: Rows 13b and 13d describe an import over a tree whose task file already carries a task-level `all` — so the target task file EXISTS — but neither states whether it holds tasks, and tp's behaviour splits on exactly that. Measured with the dev binary in /tmp/tp-r12/import: `tp import` over an existing task file that holds real tasks exits 3 with {"error":"task file already exists: spec/a.tasks.json (use --force to overwrite)","code":3} BEFORE reaching anything the fence could evaluate, and `--force` under TP_UNATTENDED=1 exits 2 with the import-force refusal. So on a tasks-bearing fixture: row 13b's assertion "is refused" is satisfied by exit 3 from the pre-existing exists-guard — the test passes green while the audit_converge_on fence is not implemented at all — and row 13d's "two documents import cleanly" cannot pass at all, because both are refused for the same unrelated reason. Only a zero-task init shell (or an absent target) reaches the change rule, which is the precondition neither row states. Row 12 pins "exits 2", so it is safe; 13b says only "is refused", which is the weaker phrasing and the one that fails open. The remaining four document shapes were all run over a zero-task shell to confirm the preconditions do work there: a `workflow` key without the field moved the resolved value from override:all to project:blocking (the refusal case, exit 0 today); omitting the key preserved override:all; carrying "audit_converge_on":"all" preserved it; and `"workflow": {}` behaved identically to the refusal case.
suggestion: State the precondition in both rows: the target is a zero-task init shell, so the import reaches the change rule rather than the exists-guard. Change row 13b's "is refused" to "exits 2 and the message is the audit_converge_on refusal", so exit 3 from the exists-guard cannot satisfy it — this is the same distinction row 14 already draws between this refusal and the command-field one. Row 13d should say the same of its clean imports (exit 0, and the task file's stored workflow still resolves `all`), since an exit-0 import that silently dropped the block would otherwise pass.

finding: Rows 21 and 22 leave their fixture under-specified in exactly the way that lets both named mutants survive. `ComputeAuditDivergence` (internal/engine/divergence.go:114-127) returns nil at condition 1 when `SpecCoverageCleanRounds` is nil or below `RequiredCleanRounds`, and at condition 5 when the latest round's stored `RolesHash` differs from `CurrentRolesHash` — both BEFORE the row walk and before condition 4. Row 21 pins only "clean and converged under `blocking` while holding non-spec-coverage rows"; row 22 says "the same fixture" with the rows carrying no `role`. A fixture satisfying those and failing condition 1 emits no object under correct code AND under "delete condition 4" AND under "exempt roleless rows from condition 4", so both rows pass on their own mutants. The engine's fixtures are hand-assembled (`newDivergenceFixture`, internal/engine/divergence_test.go:32) and `DivergenceInputs.SpecCoverageCleanRounds` is a `*int` that defaults to nil, so the passing-for-the-wrong-reason fixture is the easy one to write. §7's own standard this round is that a row states any counting rule it depends on; these two depend on two conditions they never name, and §6.5 says row 22 exists precisely "so the cost §6.5 accepts cannot change without a failing test".
suggestion: Add to both rows: "with `spec_coverage_clean_rounds` at or above the resolved `audit_clean_rounds` and the latest round's stored `roles_hash` equal to the current corpus hash — without both, conditions 1 and 5 suppress the object before condition 4 is reached and either mutant passes."

finding: Six of §7's rows (12, 13, 13b, 13c, 13d, 18) are the first in this spec whose truth depends on the AMBIENT TP_UNATTENDED of the process running the suite, and none states that dependency — which §7's own new preamble demands ("states any file, function or counting rule it depends on"). Measured, not reasoned: internal/cli's test helper builds every child as `cmd.Env = append(append(os.Environ(), "NO_COLOR=1", "TP_HC=0"), extra...)` (runTPEnv, internal/cli/run_driver_test.go), so it INHERITS the parent's TP_UNATTENDED. Running `TP_UNATTENDED=1 go test ./internal/cli -count=1` today produces 20+ failures that do not occur attended, including TestImport_WorkflowPreserved (all three subtests — the exact preservation mechanism §3's remedy 1 depends on), every TestSkipGate_*, TestImport_ConvergenceEnforced/force_bypasses_both_checks, and all four TestUnattendedFence_* guards. So "with TP_UNATTENDED unset" (row 13c) is not achieved by a test that merely does not set it. This is not hypothetical for this release: REFERENCE.md and CLAUDE.md both state tp run gives every child TP_UNATTENDED=1, and the project quality gate a run's implement unit executes is `go test -count=1 -race ./...` — so under tp run, the release's primary self-development model, these rows would run in the wrong mode. Row 18 is the sharpest case because it converts a currently env-INSENSITIVE guard into an env-sensitive one: TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate was run both ways just now and passes both (it asserts a NON-zero exit and "unknown workflow field"), but its reversal to "audit_converge_on IS a known workflow field" asserts that `tp set --workflow --project audit_converge_on=blocking` succeeds over a fixture with no task-level override — a write that changes the resolved value to blocking and therefore exits 2 under the very fence row 12 adds.
suggestion: State the dependency in the rows and make it mechanical. Every row scoped to the fence should say the environment is set EXPLICITLY per invocation rather than inherited: rows 12/13/13b/13d pass TP_UNATTENDED=1, and row 13c must actively UNSET it (an explicit removal from the child env, not an omission) or the inherited value silently inverts it. Row 18's reversed assertions need the same treatment, and the row should say so, because it is the row that turns an env-neutral guard into an env-dependent one. If the wider inheritance is out of scope for this release, say that too — but the six rows this release writes cannot be left to inherit.

finding: Two of row 18's three clauses cannot be written as a deterministic assertion. The row asserts that `TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate` "still holds **eleven** `assert.`/`require.` call sites; the two naming `audit_converge_on` now assert it **is** a known workflow field, and the other nine are byte-identical". The count is writable as a source-scanning guard (verified against the tree: internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go lines 473, 474, 481, 484, 485, 490, 493, 494, 497, 498, 500 — eleven, of which 473 and 474 name the field). "Byte-identical" names no baseline: a test written after the edit holds no pre-release copy of the nine, so the property is checkable only by reading the diff, which is review rather than a test. "Now assert it **is** a known workflow field" is a claim about what an assertion means, not about a value any assertion can compare. Three engineers write three different tests — one counts, one embeds nine literals, one drops the clauses — and only the first can fail.
suggestion: Keep the count clause and replace the other two with what a test can hold: "and the nine surviving sites still assert the same three subjects — a `wontfix` disposition does not clear `go-safety`'s open finding, `--status --check` still exits 1, and a streak entry carries exactly `role`, `consecutive_clean` and `open`". For the reversal itself, assert the behaviour (`tp set --workflow --project audit_converge_on=blocking` exits 0 attended) rather than the assertion's wording.

finding: §7's closing paragraph presents its list of untested surfaces as complete ("Not tested here, named so the absence is deliberate") and names only `role_streaks[].open`, `consecutive_clean` and `spec_coverage_clean_rounds`. At least three decisions the spec makes normatively are pinned by no row and appear in no absence list. suggestion: Add a row for the not-yet-converged branch (the same fixture as row 10, one round earlier, asserting the count appears in the non-converged string too). Add a row or an explicit acceptance pointer for §2.1's SKILL.md command. Add one sentence to §7's closing paragraph saying the §6 sweep is verified in task acceptance rather than by a test, so the absence reads as deliberate.

finding: The header states this file is decisions and that forensics belong in task acceptance, then three passages narrate the drafting rather than the decision: §2's seven lines on what 'an earlier draft wrote' and the word `surviving` being deleted 'for imprecision'; §2's 'two earlier drafts left it to be inferred and both inferred it wrong'; and §6's 'The count has been one, two, three and five, and each number was falsified by the next round'.
